name: Lansquenet
description: Lansquenet (from the French spelling of German 'Landsknecht' meaning 'servant of the land') is one of the oldest recorded banking card games, dating to at least 1542. It is an extremely simple gambling game where players bet on whether a player card or the dealer's card will appear first from the deck. Purely a game of chance with no skill involved, it was notorious in European military camps and royal courts for its rapid betting and potential for large losses.

overview.description: Lansquenet (from the French spelling of German 'Landsknecht' meaning 'servant of the land') is one of the oldest recorded banking card games, dating to at least 1542. It is an extremely simple gambling game where players bet on whether a player card or the dealer's card will appear first from the deck. Purely a game of chance with no skill involved, it was notorious in European military camps and royal courts for its rapid betting and potential for large losses.

history.origins: Developed by the Landsknechts, the colorful and violent mercenary pikemen of the Holy Roman Empire, around 1480-1500. The game was first documented in the 1542 edition of Rabelais' Gargantua and Pantagruel.
timeline: 1500s: The primary pastime in European military camps; soldiers would gamble their pay within hours of receiving it.
1600s: Spread to the French court under Louis XIII and XIV, where it was often banned due to nobles being bankrupted.
1700s: Became a staple in casinos and clandestine gambling halls across Europe.
Present: Largely extinct as a living game, except as historical reenactment or featured in literature and film (notably Stanley Kubrick's 'Barry Lyndon').
history.cultural: In historical literature, Lansquenet is synonymous with high-stakes desperation and military bravado. It represents the chaotic, all-or-nothing gambling culture of Renaissance mercenaries. The game required no skill, making it accessible to illiterate soldiers and aristocrats alike.
history.evolution: The game was traditionally played with multiple decks shuffled together to decrease the chance of ties and increase betting duration. Various regional rules developed regarding when the bank could be passed.

setup.players: One Banker (Dealer) and any number of bettors. Minimum 2 players total.
setup.deck: Standard 52-card deck. Multiple decks (2-4) are often shuffled together to reduce ties.
setup.dealing: The banker shuffles the deck(s) and places them in a shoe or pile. No cards are dealt to players initially.
setup.equipment: Cards and a flat surface. A 'shoe' or dealing box is traditionally used.

rules.objective: Bet on whether the 'Player' card or the 'Banker' card will appear first as cards are turned up from the deck.
rules.gameplay: 1. **Banker Card**: The banker turns up one card from the deck and places it on their right (The Banker's Card). 2. **Player Card**: The banker turns up a second card and places it on the left (The Player's Card). 3. **Initial Tie**: If these two cards match in rank, the banker wins all bets immediately. 4. **The Draw**: The banker continues turning up cards from the deck one by one. - If a card matches the Banker's Card rank, the banker wins all bets. - If a card matches the Player's Card rank, the banker pays all bettors at even money.
keyRules: Only card ranks matter; suits are irrelevant.
If the first two cards match (tie), banker wins immediately.
The first matching card dealt determines the winner.
Bets are typically placed after seeing the first two cards but before the draw begins.
Multiple decks reduce the frequency of ties.

strategy.basic: There is no strategy. The game is purely mathematical chance with no player decisions affecting the outcome. The only 'choice' is whether to play at a table where the banker's bank is large enough to cover potential payouts.
strategy.intermediate: Money Management: Since Lansquenet is a 'fast' game with rapid resolution, set a strict loss limit before playing. Historically, experienced gamblers would 'fold' (stop betting) after three consecutive wins to protect their stack.
strategy.advanced: Theoretical Card Counting: In theory, if playing with a single deck and cards are not reshuffled between rounds, one could track which ranks have been depleted. However, with multiple decks (the standard), this is practically impossible.
tips: If you are the Banker, your edge is entirely in the initial deal. If you don't hit a matching pair in the first two cards, your odds drop to approximately 50-50.
The faster the game is played, the more dangerous it is for your bankroll. Take your time between rounds.
Never chase losses in a pure chance gameâ€”the odds don't 'owe' you anything.
